meta.title: Alignment Through Games
meta.thesis: How do you get a learning system to want what you meant? Build games where it doesn't.
meta.scope: Reinforcement learning is the means: how agents learn rules and pursue goals. The alignment control problem is the lens: why the goal they learn is often not the one we intended, and what we can do about it. Every concept is learned through a game you build, play, or break.

arc.label: Rules
arc.text: How an agent learns what the world does in response to its actions.

arc.label: Goals
arc.text: How a number, the reward, turns into behavior that looks like wanting something.

arc.label: Misspecification
arc.text: Why that number almost never says exactly what we meant, and how optimizers find the gap.

arc.label: Control
arc.text: How to keep a system safe and correctable when we can't fully trust what it learned to want.

method.title: Weekly rhythm
points: 1.5 h theory: read, watch, and work the math by hand.
2 h lab: build, train, or break something in a game.
0.5 h note: one atomic concept note in your own words.

method.title: Done-checks
points: Every module ends with a concrete, checkable result, not a feeling of understanding.
Plus a one-page "explain it to a friend" memo. If you can't write it, you're not done.

method.title: Rules of the road
points: Implement before you import: write each algorithm from scratch once, then use the library.
Predict before you train: write down what you expect, then compare.
Everything runs on a laptop. Cloud is optional and capped.

modules.title: Agents, Games, and the Reward Hypothesis
modules.big_question: What does it mean for a machine to "have a goal", and why is a score never quite the goal?

theory.title: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.), ch. 1 and 3
theory.note: The agent–environment loop, MDPs, returns, and the reward hypothesis. Free online.

theory.title: Brian Christian, The Alignment Problem: Introduction and Part II (Agency), first chapter
theory.note: The story of RL, from Thorndike's cats to Atari, told for humans.

theory.title: Manheim & Garrabrant (2018), Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law
theory.note: Four distinct ways a measure stops being a good target. Keep this taxonomy all year.

theory.title: Bowling et al. (2022), Settling the Reward Hypothesis
theory.note: Deep dive: exactly which goals can and can't be expressed as a scalar reward.

theory.title: Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning, ch. 5–6
theory.note: Math refresh: vector calculus and probability. Skim; return when needed.

lab.title: Build your first world
lab.summary: Design and build a tiny gridworld game. It becomes your test subject for the whole year.
steps: Design an 8×8 grid game with an agent, a goal, a hazard, and one collectible coin.
Implement it as a gymnasium.Env (reset, step, ASCII and RGB render).
Play it yourself with the keyboard. Write down what "winning" means in plain English.
Write a reward function that you believe encodes that intent.
Before any training, write a one-paragraph prediction of how an optimizer could score high without doing what you meant. You'll test it in Module 4.

reflection: Is your reward a description of what you want, or a measurement of it?
What does the Markov property assume about your game, and where would it break?
Name a game you've played where you "won" without doing what the designer intended.

modules.title: Tabular RL: Learning From Reward
modules.big_question: How can an agent discover good behavior purely from trial, error, and a number?

theory.title: Sutton & Barto, ch. 2, 4, 5, 6
theory.note: Bandits, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning. The core of the field.

theory.title: David Silver, UCL RL course, lectures 1–5
theory.note: The classic lecture companion to Sutton & Barto.

theory.title: Brian Christian, The Alignment Problem: Part II (Agency), remaining chapters
theory.note: Dopamine as a TD error signal, shaping, and curiosity.

lab.title: Casino, maze, blackjack
lab.summary: Every classic tabular algorithm, from scratch, each one in a game. numpy only, no RL libraries.
steps: 10-armed bandit testbed: ε-greedy vs. UCB. Reproduce the shape of Sutton & Barto Figure 2.2.
Value iteration and policy iteration on your Module 0 gridworld. Render the value map as a heatmap.
Monte Carlo control on Gymnasium's Blackjack-v1. Compare with the book's optimal policy chart.
Q-learning and SARSA on FrozenLake and Cliff Walking. See why SARSA takes the safe path (Example 6.6).

done_check: Learning curves qualitatively match the book's figures.
Value maps and policies are plotted for your gridworld.
The Cliff Walking SARSA-vs-Q-learning difference is explained in your own words.
reflection: Q-learning hugs the cliff edge; SARSA avoids it. Which is "correct"?
What does the discount factor say about what the agent values?
Where did your agent's behavior surprise you?

modules.title: Deep RL: Policies That Generalize
modules.big_question: What changes when the world is too big for a table and the agent has to generalize?

theory.title: Mnih et al. (2015), Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning (DQN)
theory.note: One network, 49 Atari games, raw pixels.

theory.title: OpenAI Spinning Up: Parts 1–3
theory.note: Key concepts, the algorithm taxonomy, and a clean derivation of the policy gradient.

theory.title: Schulman et al. (2017), Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
theory.note: The workhorse algorithm, also used in RLHF.

theory.title: Huang et al. (2022), The 37 Implementation Details of PPO
theory.note: Why your PPO doesn't work yet.

theory.title: CleanRL, single-file ppo.py
theory.note: Read it line by line before writing your own.

theory.title: ARENA, Reinforcement Learning chapter
theory.note: Guided exercises: Q-learning, DQN, policy gradients, PPO.

lab.title: From CartPole to your world
lab.summary: Scale from tables to neural networks, then point them at your own game.
steps: DQN on CartPole-v1 in PyTorch (CPU or Apple MPS).
Copy CleanRL's ppo.py and annotate every line.
Reimplement PPO from your annotations, without looking.
Train PPO on MiniGrid-DoorKey-5x5, then on your own gridworld.
Keep a run log: what you changed, why, and what happened.

done_check: Your PPO hits CleanRL's CartPole reward threshold within 2× its sample count.
reflection: What is the deadly triad, and which parts of DQN fight it?
Why does PPO clip?
Your agent learned a policy. Did it learn the rules of the game? How would you tell?

modules.title: Planning, Self-Play, and Learned Rules
modules.big_question: Can an agent learn the rules of a game it was never told, and plan inside them?

theory.title: Tesauro (1995), Temporal Difference Learning and TD-Gammon
theory.note: Self-play reaches world-class backgammon, three decades early.

theory.title: Silver et al. (2017), Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play (AlphaZero)
theory.note: Given the rules, learn everything else.

theory.title: Schrittwieser et al. (2020), Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model (MuZero)
theory.note: Not even given the rules. It learns a model of them.

theory.title: Sutton & Barto, ch. 8: Planning and Learning (incl. MCTS)
theory.note: Model-based RL, Dyna, and Monte Carlo tree search.

theory.title: Lanctot et al. (2019), OpenSpiel
theory.note: The game framework you'll use.

lab.title: Connect Four dojo
lab.summary: Build a self-taught Connect Four player on a laptop.
steps: Play Connect Four in OpenSpiel against random and MCTS bots.
Implement MCTS (UCT) yourself and compare it with OpenSpiel's.
Tiny AlphaZero: a small policy-value net, MCTS, and a self-play loop.
Stretch: a MuZero-style learned dynamics model for tic-tac-toe. Does it predict illegal moves?

done_check: Your agent beats random >99% and MCTS-50 >90% over 200 games.
reflection: AlphaZero was given the rules; MuZero learned a model of them. What's gained, and what's at risk?
Self-play optimizes winning. What else could "winning" have been measured as?

modules.title: The Control Problem I: Specification
modules.big_question: Why do agents find ways to score that their designers never intended, and what can we do about it?

theory.title: Amodei et al. (2016), Concrete Problems in AI Safety
theory.note: The founding taxonomy: side effects, reward hacking, oversight, safe exploration, distribution shift.

theory.title: Leike et al. (2017), AI Safety Gridworlds
theory.note: Safety problems as tiny games. Your lab rebuilds them.

theory.title: Krakovna et al., Specification gaming examples in AI
theory.note: The master list, CoastRunners included. Read ten entries a week.

theory.title: Skalse et al. (2022), Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking
theory.note: A formal answer to when a proxy reward is "unhackable". Almost never.

theory.title: Ng, Harada & Russell (1999), Policy Invariance Under Reward Transformations
theory.note: Potential-based shaping: the one kind of reward change that provably can't be gamed.

theory.title: Krakovna et al. (2018), Penalizing Side Effects Using Stepwise Relative Reachability
theory.note: Impact measures: don't break the vase.

theory.title: Orseau & Armstrong (2016), Safely Interruptible Agents
theory.note: Can an agent learn not to resist being stopped?

theory.title: Hadfield-Menell et al. (2017), The Off-Switch Game
theory.note: Uncertainty about the goal is what makes an agent let you switch it off.

theory.title: Stuart Russell, Human Compatible
theory.note: The control problem, stated by one of the authors of the standard AI textbook.

lab.title: The hack gallery
lab.summary: Rebuild DeepMind's safety gridworlds, watch your agent cheat, then try to stop it.
steps: Rebuild four AI Safety Gridworlds as MiniGrid environments: Off-Switch, Absent Supervisor, Irreversible Side Effects, Tomato Watering. The original repo is archived; the paper specifies each one.
Give each environment a hidden performance function separate from the reward, as in the paper.
Train your PPO and record a GIF of every way it games the reward.
Revisit your Module 0 prediction. Was it right?
Implement one fix per environment (potential-based shaping, an impact penalty, randomized supervision) and measure reward vs. hidden performance.

done_check: A gallery page with, per environment: failure GIF, fix GIF, a reward-vs-performance table, and a paragraph on why the fix works or doesn't.
reflection: Was each failure a bug in the agent, in the reward, or in your intent?
Why does potential-based shaping provably leave the optimal policy unchanged?
When an agent lets you switch it off, is it safe, or just indifferent?

modules.title: The Control Problem II: Learned Goals
modules.big_question: If we can't write the goal down, can the agent learn it from us, and what goes wrong when it does?

theory.title: Christiano et al. (2017), Deep RL from Human Preferences
theory.note: Learn the reward from comparisons. The ancestor of RLHF.

theory.title: Ouyang et al. (2022), Training Language Models to Follow Instructions (InstructGPT)
theory.note: RLHF at scale.

theory.title: Rafailov et al. (2023), Direct Preference Optimization
theory.note: Preference learning without an explicit reward model.

theory.title: Gao, Schulman & Hilton (2022), Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
theory.note: Goodhart, measured: the proxy rises while the true reward falls.

theory.title: Hubinger et al. (2019), Risks from Learned Optimization
theory.note: Inner vs. outer alignment; mesa-optimizers.

theory.title: Langosco et al. (2022), Goal Misgeneralization in Deep RL
theory.note: The CoinRun agent that learned "go right" instead of "get the coin".

theory.title: Shah et al. (2022), Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough
theory.note: Even a perfect reward can produce the wrong goal.

theory.title: Brian Christian, The Alignment Problem: Part III (Normativity)
theory.note: Imitation, inference, and uncertainty.

lab.title: You are the human labeler
lab.summary: Teach an agent your goal through preferences, then watch it learn something else.
steps: Record short clip pairs of agents playing your gridworld; label your preferences in a tiny CLI.
Train a Bradley–Terry reward model on your labels.
Run PPO against the learned reward, with and without a KL penalty to a reference policy.
Plot learned reward vs. your true intent as optimization pressure rises, and find where it turns.
Goal misgeneralization: train in MiniGrid with the key always in one corner, then move it. Does the agent chase the corner or the key?
Optional (≤$10 cloud): ARENA's RLHF exercises on a small language model.

done_check: A memo explains outer vs. inner misalignment using your own results.
reflection: Your preferences were noisy and inconsistent. What did the reward model learn instead?
In the corner experiment, was the reward wrong? Was the training wrong?
What would convince you that an agent pursues the goal you meant, not a proxy that happened to coincide during training?

modules.title: Looking Inside: Did It Learn the Rules?
modules.big_question: When a network plays well, has it built an internal model of the game, and can we read it?

theory.title: Li et al. (2022), Emergent World Representations (Othello-GPT)
theory.note: A model trained only on move sequences builds a board inside.

theory.title: Nanda, Lee & Wattenberg (2023), Emergent Linear Representations in World Models
theory.note: The board is linear if you encode it as "mine/theirs".

theory.title: Jenner et al. (2024), Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
theory.note: Leela Chess Zero represents future moves internally.

theory.title: ARENA, interpretability chapter
theory.note: Guided exercises on probing and intervening in game-playing transformers.

lab.title: Probe the board
lab.summary: Train a small transformer on Othello and find the board inside it.
steps: Generate synthetic legal Othello games with a random player.
Train a small transformer (a few million parameters) to predict legal next moves on a laptop.
Train linear probes on its activations to recover the board. Compare "black/white" vs. "mine/theirs" encodings.
Intervene: edit the probed board representation and see whether predicted moves change.
Bonus: probe your Module 5 agent for a representation of the goal location.

done_check: Probe accuracy is well above a randomly initialized baseline.
One intervention changes move predictions as expected.
A memo on what "learned the rules" actually means.
reflection: Why did "mine/theirs" probe better than "black/white"?
Is a linearly decodable board the same as the model "knowing" the board?
Could interpretability have caught Module 5's goal misgeneralization before deployment?

modules.title: Frontier & Capstone: Control as a Game
modules.big_question: If we can't fully trust what a capable system wants, can we still design protocols that keep it safe?

theory.title: Irving, Christiano & Amodei (2018), AI Safety via Debate
theory.note: Oversight as a two-player zero-sum game.

theory.title: Greenblatt et al. (2023), AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
theory.note: Safety protocols evaluated as red team vs. blue team.

theory.title: Greenblatt et al. (2024), Alignment Faking in Large Language Models
theory.note: A model that behaves differently when it believes it's being trained.

theory.title: METR (2025), Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
theory.note: Frontier models tampering with scorers on real evaluation tasks.

theory.title: MacDiarmid et al. (2025), Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL
theory.note: Learning to hack generalized to sabotage and alignment faking.

theory.title: Bai et al. (2022), Constitutional AI
theory.note: Feedback from principles instead of per-example human labels.

lab.title: Capstone: the rigged arena
lab.summary: Build a game whose scorer can be cheated, catch the cheater, and publish what you learn.
steps: Design a game where an agent is scored by a judge it can tamper with: a scoring bug, an editable flag, a blind spot.
Train an agent and confirm it learns to exploit the judge.
Blue team: design a control protocol, such as a trusted monitor, budgeted audits, or randomized checks.
Red team: adapt the agent (or a scripted adversary) to evade your monitor. Measure safety vs. usefulness, as in the AI Control paper.
Write it up publicly: the game, the hack, the protocol, what held and what broke.

done_check: A safety-vs-usefulness plot for at least two protocols.
reflection: What would change if the agent could read your monitor's code?
Which of your Module 4 fixes would survive a smarter optimizer?
After a year: what is the control problem, in one paragraph, in your own words?
